title: Q&A: What does China’s 15th ‘five-year plan’ for renewables mean for climate change? - Carbon Brief
gist: China's 2026-2030 renewables five-year plan (NDRC/NEA, published late July 2026) targets 3,500GW of renewable capacity and 2,800GW of wind and solar by 2030 — but that implies only ~160GW/year of wind and solar additions versus 315GW of solar alone installed in 2025, making the headline number a deceleration, not an acceleration. The plan's genuine novelty is qualitative: first-ever 'firm capacity' targets (11% for wind, 6% for solar) that could displace the peak-demand justification for new coal plants, plus a near-tripling of non-power renewable use to 150Mtce centred on green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol.

insights.claim: China's 15th five-year plan targets 3,500GW of total renewables capacity by 2030, of which 2,800GW is wind and solar — more than double the previous 1,200GW wind-and-solar target that China hit six years early.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Sets the ceiling for the world's largest renewables procurement pipeline through 2030; every module, turbine and inverter supplier's TAM assumption keys off this number.
insights.quote: China will aim to install 3,500 gigawatts (GW) of renewables capacity by 2030, according to the five-year plan.
insights.locator: What overarching renewables targets are in the plan?

insights.claim: Meeting China's 2030 wind-and-solar target requires only about 160GW of additions per year, versus 277GW of new solar alone in 2024 and 315GW in 2025 — meaning the official plan sanctions roughly a halving of the recent build rate.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The 'doubled' headline target is actually a floor far below run-rate; Chinese solar manufacturers should not read the plan as demand support, and overcapacity/pricing pressure in polysilicon, wafer and module chains is unlikely to be resolved by domestic policy pull.
insights.quote: China would need to build 160GW of wind and solar each year
insights.locator: As such, China would need to build

insights.claim: As of June 2026 China had installed just under 2,000GW of wind and solar plus 454GW of hydropower, leaving roughly 800GW of wind-and-solar headroom against the 2,800GW 2030 goal.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Baseline for sizing the remaining four-and-a-half-year domestic order book; the gap is small enough that surplus Chinese manufacturing capacity must find export markets.
insights.locator: As of June 2026, the country has installed

insights.claim: The plan targets 6,000TWh of renewable generation by 2030 (4,000TWh from wind and solar), a 50% rise from just under 4,000TWh in 2025, with the wind-and-solar component growing 74% from 2,300TWh.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Generation growth outpacing capacity growth implies planners expect higher utilisation and lower curtailment — a testable claim against monthly NEA curtailment data.
insights.locator: the plan sets a target for renewable power generation

insights.claim: Renewable energy consumption is targeted to rise from 1.2Gtce in 2025 to 1.8Gtce in 2030, against total Chinese energy consumption of 6.2Gtce in 2025 — meaning renewables were only about one-fifth of the primary energy mix at the plan's start.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Frames how much fossil demand is still in place; even a fully delivered plan leaves the majority of Chinese primary energy non-renewable in 2030.
insights.locator: By 2030, the plan says that total consumption of renewable energy

insights.claim: Hydropower capacity is set to grow from 448GW in 2025 to 570GW in 2030, with 160GW of that being pumped storage — an implied jump from 66GW, or +142%, making pumped hydro the fastest-growing large-scale storage class in the plan.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A ~94GW pumped-storage build implies heavy civil-engineering, turbine and grid-connection spend, and competes directly with battery storage for the same balancing revenue pool.
insights.locator: China will also add more hydropower

insights.claim: The plan's small-technology growth rates are the steepest in percentage terms: solar thermal from 1.8GW to 15GW (+733%) and renewable hydrogen from 0.25Mt to 2Mt (+700%), versus roughly 50% growth for headline wind, solar and generation metrics.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Percentage upside sits in the niches, not the majors — where Chinese policy pull is strongest relative to a tiny base, and where equipment suppliers face the least incumbent competition.
insights.locator: Key targets for 2030, adapted from 15th five-year plan

insights.claim: The plan's renewables targets fall below what a Tsinghua University study says is required, with that study finding China must either install more than 4,000GW of non-fossil capacity before 2030 or hold total energy consumption below 6.5Gtce to meet its climate commitments.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
entities: Institute of Climate Change and Sustainable Development
insights.so_what: Signals that the carbon-peak trajectory now hinges on energy-demand restraint rather than supply build-out — watch total energy consumption prints, not just capacity adds, as the binding variable.
insights.quote: China would need to either install more than 4,000GW of “non-fossil energy capacity” before 2030, or to “maintain a total energy consumption” below 6.5Gtce.
insights.locator: The renewable targets in the plan are lower

themes.theme: Firm capacity as the new metric

insights.claim: China's renewables plan introduces 'firm capacity' (置信出力) targets for the first time: wind must deliver at least 11% of installed capacity and solar 6% during critical supply periods by 2030, in conjunction with on-site storage.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Creates a de facto co-located storage mandate — project economics now require batteries attached to new wind and solar, expanding the addressable storage market independently of standalone storage policy.
insights.quote: The target for wind is a firm capacity of at least 11% of total installed capacity by 2030, while the equivalent goal for solar is 6%.
insights.locator: Why does the plan focus on ‘firm capacity’ for renewables?

insights.claim: Wind and solar are required to supply more than 20% of total demand during summer and winter evening peaks, with 'reliable peak-shaving capacity from renewable sources' reaching over 300GW by 2030.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A 300GW dispatchable-renewables goal is the clearest quantified demand signal in the plan for storage, grid-forming inverters and flexible dispatch assets.
insights.locator: Wind and solar will also be expected to supply

insights.claim: Because firm-capacity targets apply only during peak load and critical supply periods — the exact window used to justify new coal plants — they could in theory block coal projects approved on peak-demand grounds, according to Greenpeace East Asia's Yao Zhe.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The single most consequential second-order effect in the plan: if enforced, it caps China's coal approval pipeline and reprices thermal-coal demand expectations; watch provincial coal approval counts as the read-through.
insights.quote: prevent the construction of new coal-fired power projects that are proposed and approved for the reason of meeting peak demand
insights.locator: The new targets are a “positive move”

insights.claim: Lyu Wenbin, director general of the NDRC's Energy Research Institute, frames the plan as a shift from pursuing installed capacity to also valuing system support capability — an explicit move away from GW-counting as the metric of success.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals policy support migrating from module/turbine volume toward grid services, storage and power electronics — rotate exposure from commodity manufacturing to system-integration value.
insights.quote: marks a shift in renewable energy development from the mere pursuit of installed capacity to…also taking into account system support capabilities
insights.locator: The new metrics mark a change in focus

insights.claim: The plan splits its grid strategy geographically: 'grid-friendly' wind and solar stations with reliable peak-load generation are targeted at the energy-hungry east, central and south, while high-renewables regions like north-west China are told to build parks providing voltage, frequency and inertia support.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Two distinct equipment demand profiles by region — load-following plus storage in the load centres, grid-forming inverters and synchronous condensers in the north-west.
insights.locator: It sets out a slightly different focus for areas

insights.claim: The plan lists many technological solutions for grid stability but sets no quantitative goal — for example no target for how many gigawatts of wind and solar must gain grid-forming capability — in sharp contrast to its precise capacity and generation targets, according to GEM's James Norman.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Absence of a numeric mandate means grid-forming inverter demand stays discretionary and provincially driven — a weaker investment signal than the storage-implying firm-capacity rules.
insights.quote: how many gigawatts of wind and solar must gain grid-forming capability
insights.locator: The plan mentions many technological solutions

insights.claim: Coal still generates 42% of the power transmitted from China's large-scale clean-energy megabases to the rest of the country, paired with renewables in the name of balancing and system flexibility, per a Global Energy Monitor report.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: UHV transmission build-out is not a pure renewables trade — it currently underwrites coal offtake, and the plan's aspiration to push megabase renewable share to 100% is only 'further research', not a target.
insights.quote: continues to be paired with coal-fired generation in the name of balancing and system flexibility
insights.locator: A recent report by the thinktank Global Energy Monitor

insights.claim: Renewable power — especially solar — is increasingly being curtailed in north-western and northern Chinese provinces because of transmission bottlenecks plus systemic features such as dispatching and power-contract mechanisms, per Global Energy Monitor.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Curtailment is a contractual and dispatch problem, not only a wires problem — meaning realised IRRs on northern solar can deteriorate even as transmission capacity is added.
insights.locator: As a result, said the report, renewable power

insights.claim: The plan avoids specific measures to address systemic grid constraints and the role of coal in the power sector, which Greenpeace East Asia's Yao Zhe reads as evidence that vested interests remain strong in the policy debate.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Implies coal-fired generation retains structural protection through 2030 regardless of renewables targets — a reason to discount aggressive Chinese coal-demand decline forecasts.
insights.quote: I interpret this as evidence that the vested interests are still strong in the policy debate
insights.locator: Yao also notes that the plan does not

insights.claim: The plan calls for more than 300GW of distributed new energy over 2026-30, about 60GW per year, but distributed solar additions alone exceeded 100GW in both 2024 and 2025 — so the target is not overly ambitious, says Transition Asia's Isadora Wang.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Confirms the deceleration pattern extends to distributed generation; rooftop-solar installers and inverter suppliers should model a shrinking Chinese market, not a growing one.
insights.locator: The 60GW annual target for new distributed energy

insights.claim: Market conditions for Chinese distributed solar have deteriorated sharply over the past two years through growing exposure to market trading, worsening spot-market returns, rising curtailment risk and new policies limiting or forbidding selling power back to the grid, according to Trivium China's Cosimo Ries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Four simultaneous negative drivers on distributed solar IRR — the binding constraint on Chinese module demand is now returns and offtake rules, not policy targets or panel prices.
insights.quote: growing exposure to market trading, worsening returns in spot markets, growing risks of curtailment and new policies limiting or forbidding the selling of power back to the grid
insights.locator: He adds that market conditions for distributed solar

insights.claim: The open question on distributed energy is not the target's feasibility but whether it will continue to make economic sense for industry and utilities to build distributed power at 14th five-year-plan volumes, per Cosimo Ries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Reframes the risk: Chinese distributed demand could undershoot even a modest target if commercial buyers step back — watch monthly distributed installation data for a break below the 60GW annualised pace.
insights.locator: Cosimo Ries, analyst at the consultancy Trivium China

insights.claim: Distributed solar and wind is likely to meet a large proportion of local demand in some Chinese regions, with micro- and mini-grids particularly important in central and coastal China, says Prof Pan Jiahua of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
entities: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
insights.so_what: Microgrid controls, local storage and behind-the-meter equipment become the growth niche in coastal load centres even as utility-scale additions slow.
insights.locator: In some regions, distributed solar and wind

insights.claim: The plan directs distributed energy into industrial parks, coal mines and oilfields as well as buildings and rural clean-energy grids, extending renewables into fossil-extraction sites themselves.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Captive-generation demand from heavy industry and extraction operators is a distinct offtake channel insulated from spot-market and grid-sale restrictions.
insights.locator: Applications include the use of distributed solar and wind

themes.theme: Non-power renewables: hydrogen and heavy industry

insights.claim: China targets non-power use of renewables rising from 60Mtce in 2025 to 150Mtce in 2030 — a near-tripling from a base of only about 1% of total Chinese energy consumption today.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The fastest-growing pillar of the plan in relative terms; electrolyser, industrial heat and e-fuel suppliers get an explicit national demand signal for the first time.
insights.locator: What does the plan say about non-electricity use of renewables?

insights.claim: China plans to scale renewable hydrogen production from 250,000 tonnes in 2025 to 2m tonnes by 2030, with green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol described as the centrepiece of the non-power push by state-owned Economic Information Daily.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: An eight-fold green hydrogen ramp implies tens of GW of electrolyser orders and makes China the price-setter in green ammonia and methanol just as shipping and fertiliser buyers seek supply.
insights.locator: For hydrogen alone, China plans to scale up

insights.claim: The plan directs new steel and cement projects to use locally-generated wind and solar to power electric-arc furnaces and kilns, and envisages centralised wind and solar heating stations for chemicals, textiles, pharmaceuticals, papermaking and food.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Named sectors get first-mover compliance costs and captive renewables demand — a screen for which Chinese industrial subsectors face incoming energy-sourcing mandates.
insights.locator: New projects in the steel and cement sectors

insights.claim: Naming individual industrial sectors in the plan is a clear indication they will be added to China's renewable consumption quotas, which already cover aluminium and other heavy industry, says Transition Asia's Isadora Wang.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Quota extension turns a soft plan mention into a hard compliance obligation for steel, chemicals and cement producers — an input-cost and competitiveness variable to price in now.
insights.locator: Wang tells Carbon Brief that she believes the naming

insights.claim: The pivot to non-power use signals that China's decarbonisation is entering deeper waters as regulators move from easier-to-abate sectors such as aluminium to harder ones such as steel, per Trivium China's Cosimo Ries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A mental model for sequencing Chinese industrial-decarbonisation policy risk: electrification-ready sectors first, process-heat and chemistry-bound sectors next.
insights.locator: To Ries, the growing focus on non-power use

insights.claim: The plan could create a 'second growth curve' for China's new-energy industry, starting with non-power use before shifting to fuel, feedstock and heat substitution, says He Zhao, vice-president of the China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
entities: China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute
insights.so_what: Explicit official framing that domestic growth for renewables companies must come from molecules and heat, not more electrons — a strategic pivot signal for Chinese cleantech equity narratives.
insights.locator: The plan could create a “second growth curve”

insights.claim: Limited available data makes it hard to assess the ambition of the 150Mtce non-power target, and given the relative conservatism of China's other recent clean-energy targets it may be met relatively easily, per Cosimo Ries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Caution against treating the tripling as a stretch goal; the pattern across this plan is targets set below achievable run-rates.
insights.locator: Ries tells Carbon Brief that he thinks this target

insights.claim: The plan explicitly frames the next five years as a prime opportunity for China to consolidate its leading position across the entire clean-energy industrial chain, pairing that with pledges to promote free circulation of Chinese green technologies in global markets.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Confirms Beijing treats cleantech supply-chain control as strategic policy, not just industry outcome — expect continued state support even amid overcapacity and margin compression.
insights.quote: consolidate our leading position across the entire industrial chain
insights.locator: What does the plan say about China’s cleantech dominance?

insights.claim: Chinese clean-energy technology exports have been surging especially since the closure of the strait of Hormuz, and Chinese clean-energy investment in Belt and Road member states reached $20bn in the first half of 2026, also driven by the crisis.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: An energy-security shock is converting into structural Chinese cleantech export share and BRI project pipeline — a durable demand channel that offsets a slowing domestic market.
insights.quote: Chinese exports of clean-energy technologies have been surging, especially since the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
insights.locator: Chinese exports of clean-energy technologies

insights.claim: US, EU and other tariffs and pricing mechanisms aimed at curbing Chinese cleantech imports have generated Chinese pushback against what it calls 'unilateral trade measures', setting up trade friction as a persistent feature of the 2026-2030 period.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Chinese export volumes will increasingly route to non-OECD and BRI markets; model tariff-exposed versus tariff-insulated revenue mix for Chinese module and battery makers.
insights.locator: The US, EU and others have launched tariffs

insights.claim: R&D priorities named in the plan include ultra-tall wind towers, floating platforms, high-altitude wind power, perovskite and other high-efficiency solar cells, and space-solar technologies, alongside accelerated rollout of AI applications in the renewable-energy system.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A concrete list of Chinese state-backed technology bets for 2026-2030 — perovskite and floating wind are near-commercial, and Chinese state funding compresses the window for Western first-movers.
insights.locator: The plan names technologies for further development

insights.claim: The plan pledges a power market supporting 'full entry' of renewable-energy companies and tells them to plan for an increasingly market-based and competitive environment, removing the assumption of guaranteed offtake.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Merchant-price exposure becomes the default for Chinese renewables; valuation multiples for Chinese IPPs should compress toward merchant-power comparables rather than regulated-utility ones.
insights.locator: The plan also pledges to develop a power market

insights.claim: China is transitioning from a 'major energy nation' (能源大国) to an 'energy powerhouse' (能源强国) and will move to the very forefront of the global stage on clean energy in 2026-2030, venturing into uncharted territory, writes the NDRC Energy Research Institute's Lyu Wenbin.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Official framing shifting from scale to systemic advantage means the competitive threat migrates from cheap hardware to standards, system design and integrated project delivery.
insights.quote: move to the very forefront of the global stage
insights.locator: China is transitioning from a “major energy nation”

themes.theme: How the five-year plan machinery works

insights.claim: China's overarching 15th five-year plan covering 2026-2030 was published in March 2026 with binding targets for carbon intensity, the non-fossil share of energy consumption and total energy production capacity, with sector-specific plans following through the cycle.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A calendar for policy catalysts: sectoral plans drop sequentially across 2026-2030, so more energy and industry targets are still pending and tradeable.
insights.locator: Why are China’s five-year plans important?

insights.claim: The renewables plan was published in late July 2026 by the NDRC and NEA, following separate 2026 plans on the 'new-type' energy sector and a 'Beautiful China' programme bundling climate with other environmental targets.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Multiple overlapping energy plans mean no single document is definitive — cross-read them before sizing any Chinese clean-energy demand forecast.
insights.locator: It was published in late July by the National Development

insights.claim: The 2,800GW wind-and-solar figure is a reiteration of China's action plan for peaking carbon emissions released earlier in July 2026, not a fresh commitment.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Guards against double-counting the same target as two separate policy catalysts when modelling Chinese demand headlines.
insights.locator: Of this, 2,800GW will be wind and solar
